సేవింగ్స్ తో పోలిస్తే ఫిక్స్డ్ డిపాజిట్ వడ్డీ నిష్పత్తి 3:2 గా ఉండి, 7.25% ఇస్తుంది. |
[Open WAV](https://huggingface.co/maya-research/maya2-native/resolve/main/samples/te_nivedita.wav) | The Tamil sample uses **Abhay**, whose listed training languages are English and Hindi. The Telugu sample uses **Nivedita**, also trained on English and Hindi. Both demonstrate cross-lingual synthesis. Assamese is cross-lingual for every built-in voice; see [limitations](#limitations). ## Quickstart Use **Linux, Python 3.10–3.12, and an NVIDIA GPU with a driver supporting CUDA 12.8**. Start with `max_seats=1`. The documented single-seat loading peak is approximately 9.2 GB plus CUDA context; a 12 GB or larger GPU provides more room. See [hardware and memory](#hardware-and-memory) before increasing concurrency. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install "maya3[server] @ git+https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 ``` ### Generate speech ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) audio = tts.generate( "नमस्ते, आपका ऑर्डर कल पहुँच जाएगा।", lang="hi", voice="Ahana", normalize=True, ) sf.write("speech.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` `generate()` returns a mono NumPy waveform in `float32`. Model weights, the Mimi codec, and the ECAPA speaker encoder are downloaded on first use. For offline inference, cache all three first, then set `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. **Normalization differs by interface:** the HTTP and WebSocket servers enable it by default. The Python API requires `normalize=True`. It expands numbers, currency, dates, times, URLs, email addresses, and other written forms into spoken text. Check the output for unusual formats.
Stream audio as it is generated ### Stream speech ```python from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) try: with open("speech.pcm", "wb") as output: for chunk in tts.stream( "Your order has shipped and will arrive tomorrow.", lang="en", voice="Siddhant", normalize=True, ): output.write(chunk.astype(" ### Clone a voice across languages Use a clean, single-speaker reference clip and its exact transcript. Obtain the speaker's permission before cloning their voice. The reference language and the output language can differ. ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) tts.register_voice( "my_voice", ref_audio="reference.wav", # 3–10 seconds recommended ref_text="", lang="hi", # reference language ) audio = tts.generate( "வணக்கம், எப்படி இருக்கிறீர்கள்?", lang="ta", # output language voice="my_voice", normalize=True, ) sf.write("cloned_voice_tamil.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` The default cloning mode, `icl_spk`, combines the reference audio with an ECAPA speaker embedding. Clones approximate the reference voice; similarity and accent vary. A dedicated cloning benchmark is not included in this release's reported results.
Run a local HTTP and WebSocket server ### Serve over HTTP or WebSocket ```bash python -m maya3.server \ --ckpt maya-research/maya2-native \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --max-seats 1 ``` After `GET /health` reports ready, generate speech: ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"input":"Your order has shipped.","language":"en","voice":"Ahana","response_format":"wav"}' \ --output speech.wav ``` The server provides `POST /v1/audio/speech`, `WS /v1/tts/stream`, and voice registration endpoints. It has no built-in authentication; add authentication and access controls before exposing it beyond a trusted environment. See the [GitHub README](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native#serve-the-model) for clients and protocol details.
## Voices Select a built-in voice by name, for example `voice="Vaidehi"`. Names are case-insensitive, and no reference audio is needed. All 20 names describe synthetic voice personas. The training-language column lists languages with **at least one hour of training audio for that voice**. A voice can be requested in any supported language, but performance outside its listed languages is cross-lingual and may sound less native. | Voice | Profile | Training languages, ≥1 hour | |---|---|---| | **Ahana** | Young female voice, bright, youthful | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Vaidehi** | Adult female voice, calm, gentle | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Malini** | Mature female voice, steady narrator | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Charvi** | Young female voice, energetic, upbeat | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Jahnavi** | Adult female voice, warm, friendly | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or ta te` | | **Anirban** | Adult male voice, steady narrator | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Nakul** | Young male voice, bright, youthful | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Vasant** | Mature male voice, steady narrator | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or ta te` | | **Siddhant** | Adult male voice, clear, professional | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Satvik** | Young male voice, warm, friendly | `bn en gu hi kn ml mr or pa ta te` | | **Abhay** | Adult male voice, natural conversational style | `en hi` | | **Nivedita** | Adult female voice, natural conversational style | `en hi` | | **Ishwari** | Adult female voice, natural conversational style | `hi` | | **Ritvik** | Adult male voice, natural conversational style | `hi` | | **Vrinda** | Young female voice, natural conversational style | `hi` | | **Sreekar** | Adult male voice, natural conversational style | `en hi te` | | **Kayal** | Adult female voice, natural conversational style | `en ta` | | **Shaunak** | Young male voice, natural conversational style | `en hi` | | **Akshat** | Adult male voice, natural conversational style | `en hi` | | **Tanushree** | Adult female voice, natural conversational style | `en hi` | Language codes: `as` Assamese · `bn` Bengali · `en` English · `gu` Gujarati · `hi` Hindi · `kn` Kannada · `ml` Malayalam · `mr` Marathi · `or` Odia · `pa` Punjabi · `ta` Tamil · `te` Telugu. Pass only the speech text and the voice name to the API. The engine constructs the voice prompt internally; adding `Ahana:` to your text is unnecessary. Use either a built-in voice or your own reference audio for a request, rather than combining them. ## Evaluation The release was evaluated on **6,000 held-out texts across 12 languages**, producing **20.3 hours of speech**. Three ASR judges measured intelligibility; a speaker-embedding classifier measured consistency among the 20 built-in voices. **These are Maya Research's release measurements.** ASR error rates and embedding similarity capture specific aspects of quality; they do not replace human listening or measure every aspect of naturalness. Serving measurements below describe the tested hardware and workload. ### Benchmark design The release benchmark, **bench6k**, contains **6,000 held-out texts: 500 per language across 31 content categories**, including conversation, names, numbers, dates, currency, addresses, URLs, code-mixed text, tongue twisters, and prompts of 1–50 words. The release documentation states that these evaluation texts were excluded from training. The benchmark produced **20.3 hours of speech** through the server, with normalization and engine guards enabled, sampled decoding, and one seed per row. Voices were distributed across languages and categories; long inputs used the serving stack's text chunking. Three ASR systems transcribed the generated speech: - **ASR-1:** Maya's in-house Indic ASR and primary judge. - **Qwen3-ASR:** a third ASR judge. - **ASR-2:** a second in-house Indic ASR, held out from training, reward generation, and checkpoint selection. **Character error rate (CER)** compares ASR transcripts with spoken-form references. Scorer v1 uses the benchmark's normalization and script harmonization. Scorer v2 additionally harmonizes Latin and native-script spellings in code-mixed spans. The two scorers evaluate the same generated audio; lower v2 scores reflect a scoring change. | Overall CER ↓ | ASR-1 | Qwen3-ASR | ASR-2, held out | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Scorer v1 | 3.49% | 3.40% | 2.86% | | Scorer v2, additional code-mix harmonization | 2.35% | 2.22% | 1.73% | ### Results by language CER below uses **scorer v1**. Voice identity is nearest-centroid classification among the 20 built-in voices, using ECAPA embeddings from clips of at least one second. It is a closed-set identity metric, separate from zero-shot clone similarity. | Language | Code | CER ASR-1 ↓ | CER Qwen3-ASR ↓ | CER ASR-2 ↓ | Voice identity ↑ | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Assamese | `as` | 5.41% | 6.59% | 5.54% | 96.4% | | Bengali | `bn` | 2.60% | 2.83% | 2.68% | 98.5% | | English | `en` | 9.69% | 1.74% | 1.43% | 99.6% | | Gujarati | `gu` | 2.25% | 3.76% | 2.26% | 98.9% | | Hindi | `hi` | 1.52% | 2.05% | 1.57% | 99.6% | | Kannada | `kn` | 2.28% | 2.72% | 2.23% | 97.9% | | Malayalam | `ml` | 3.75% | 4.20% | 4.03% | 99.4% | | Marathi | `mr` | 1.66% | 2.09% | 1.54% | 99.1% | | Odia | `or` | 3.45% | 4.33% | 3.54% | 97.4% | | Punjabi | `pa` | 2.51% | 3.32% | 2.66% | 99.1% | | Tamil | `ta` | 4.42% | 4.55% | 4.33% | 98.1% | | Telugu | `te` | 2.29% | 2.64% | 2.53% | 99.4% | ASR-1's English CER is substantially higher than the other two judges. The release analysis attributes part of this difference to ASR-1 looping on spoken URLs such as “W W W.” All three results are retained to show judge disagreement. ### Failures and voice consistency The benchmark's **consensus failure rate** requires agreement between ASR-1 and Qwen3-ASR under the release's failure rules, covering looping, substantial insertions, very high CER, and duration-limit events. | Release measurement | Result | |---|---:| | Consensus failure rate, scorer v1 | 0.15% | | Consensus failure rate, scorer v2 | 0.03% | | Outputs reaching the absolute length cap | 0.00% | | Loops / truncations | 0.02% / 0.13% | | Built-in voice name spoken aloud | 0.00% | | Voice identity, nearest of 20 centroids | 98.6% | | Mean ECAPA similarity | 0.778 | Zero observed events apply to this finite benchmark. A consensus failure rate does not count every pronunciation error or one-judge disagreement. A separate 1,248-row named-voice evaluation reports 98.9% identity in trained languages and 98.8% cross-lingual identity. The same classifier scored 98.0% on held-out recordings of the source voices. These are task-specific measurements, rather than evidence that generated speech is more natural than recorded speech. ### Harder inputs | Category | ASR-1 CER, v1 | ASR-1 CER, v2 | |---|---:|---:| | Web addresses | 29.06% | 20.34% | | Heavy code-mix | 16.74% | 4.11% | | Code-mix | 10.60% | 3.51% | | Symbols | 6.34% | 2.49% | The code-mix gap illustrates the effect of script spelling on ASR-based scoring. Pronunciation and intelligibility still need listening evaluation, especially for names, URLs, and critical numbers. ### Streaming performance The reported release serving run used **one H100 NVL with 95 GB reported memory**, **224 concurrent WebSocket streams**, a BF16 backbone, and an FP16 depth decoder. | Metric | Reported result | |---|---:| | Concurrent streams | 224 | | Aggregate throughput | 323 seconds of audio per wall-clock second | | Time to first audio, steady state, p50 / p90 / p99 | 111 / 134 / 242 ms | | Time to first audio, complete run including ramp and drain, p50 / p99 | 115 / 774 ms | | Per-stream real-time factor at full load, p50 | 0.68 | | Observed playback stalls / serving errors | 0 / 0 | A separate single-stream H100 measurement reports approximately **14 ms to first audio** and **0.13 real-time factor**. It uses a different load condition from the 224-stream run. Real-time factor is generation time divided by audio duration; lower is faster. The release analysis attributes the complete-run latency tail partly to admission queuing during the drain phase. Latency depends on hardware, load, input length, cached state, and the serving environment; these measurements do not establish public internet or telephone latency. ## Hardware and memory The engine documentation reports the following GPU allocator measurements with a BF16 backbone, FP16 depth decoder, and **2,048 KV-cache tokens per seat**. Add approximately **0.5 GB for the CUDA context** and allow additional deployment headroom. | Concurrent seats | Steady GPU memory | Peak during loading | |---|---:|---:| | 1 | 7.7 GB | 9.2 GB | | 8 | 9.7 GB | 10.9 GB | | 16 | 11.7 GB | 12.8 GB | | 32 | 15.8 GB | 16.5 GB | `max_seats` controls allocated serving capacity and memory, even before every seat is busy. These figures describe this configuration; a checkpoint's download size is smaller than its total runtime memory requirement. See [engine documentation](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native/blob/main/docs/ENGINE.md) for configuration and hardware-specific measurements.
Architecture and audio generation ## Architecture Maya 2 Native generates discrete audio tokens autoregressively, then decodes them into speech with Mimi. | Component | Description | |---|---| | Text and audio backbone | Initialized from [Qwen3-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base); 28 layers, hidden size 2,048, 16 attention heads and 8 KV heads; extended vocabulary for language and audio tokens | | Depth decoder | Approximately 555M parameters; predicts codebooks 1–31 after the backbone predicts codebook 0 | | Audio codec | [Kyutai Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi); 32 codebooks with 2,048 entries each, at 12.5 frames per second | | Speaker conditioning | 192-dimensional [SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) embedding projected into the backbone; reference-audio conditioning for cloning | | Output | 24 kHz mono speech, 80 ms per audio frame | At each step, the backbone predicts the first codebook, the depth decoder fills the remaining codebooks, and Mimi decodes an audio frame. The engine can emit that frame while generation continues. An end-of-audio token controls normal stopping; duration and loop guards provide additional controls.
## Training data and procedure The release documentation describes a mixture of **licensed and synthetic speech with transcripts** across the 12 languages, plus text-only data used to adapt the backbone to the languages. The built-in voice personas use synthetic and licensed voice data prepared for this purpose. The preference-optimization stage used **direct preference optimization (DPO)** on model-generated candidates ranked by ASR agreement and speaker similarity. Benchmark texts were excluded from training, according to the release documentation. Dataset identities, total training hours, detailed per-language composition, and the full training configuration are not disclosed in this release. Automated scores should be considered alongside these disclosure limits. ## Limitations - **Uneven language coverage.** Assamese is the most challenging Indic language in the release benchmark. No built-in voice has at least one hour of Assamese training data; some outputs drift toward a Bengali-like timbre. Other cross-lingual combinations can also carry the voice's training-language accent. - **Very short turns.** One- or two-word prompts are less stable in voice identity, and speaker-embedding evaluation is less reliable on very short clips. A slightly longer phrase may help short agent responses. - **Code-mixed and written-form inputs.** English words inside Indic sentences vary by voice. URLs, symbols, dates, and long digit sequences remain difficult, even with normalization. Listen to application-specific examples before relying on them. - **Voice cloning.** Similarity is approximate. Noise, multiple speakers, short references, and inaccurate transcripts can degrade results. Dedicated zero-shot cloning scores are not reported here. - **Emotion and events.** Tags such as `[laughs]`, `[sighs]`, `[whispers]`, `[sad]`, and `[excited]` are best effort and were not the focus of this release. - **Generation and guards.** Sampling can produce errors. The same seed is reproducible for an isolated request, but batching changes the random stream. Loop and duration guards can end genuinely repetitive text early. No benchmark clip spoke a built-in voice name aloud, but this remains a possible failure mode. - **Evaluation scope.** Results use automated ASR and speaker-embedding judges. This card does not report a human naturalness study, comprehensive dialect or demographic evaluation, confidence intervals, or a controlled comparison with other TTS models. ## Intended use and responsible deployment Maya 2 Native is intended for voice interfaces and agents, accessibility, reading and narration, IVR, notifications, and research on multilingual speech generation. Clone only voices you own or have explicit permission to use. Disclose synthetic speech to listeners, especially in calls and media. Do not use the model for deceptive impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual content, disinformation, or attempts to defeat voice authentication. Built-in voice names identify synthetic personas and should not be presented as real people. **This release does not add an audio watermark.** Applications should implement the consent, disclosure, access controls, and abuse monitoring appropriate to their use. Consult the repository's [security guidance](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for deployment considerations.
Files in this repository ## Files in this repository | Path | Contents | |---|---| | `model-00001-of-00002.safetensors`, `model-00002-of-00002.safetensors` | BF16 model weight shards | | `model.safetensors.index.json` | Weight-to-shard mapping | | `maya3_config.json` | Resolved model configuration and serialization metadata | | `backbone/` | Backbone configuration and tokenizer; backbone weights are included in the main model shards | | `voices/voices.json` | Built-in voice metadata and conditioning modes | | `samples/` | The twelve WAV examples above | Tied weights are stored once and represented through aliases. Mimi and the ECAPA speaker encoder are resolved from their own repositories on first use.

--- license: cc-by-4.0 language: - hi - te - en library_name: moshi pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio base_model: kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16 tags: - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - spoken-dialogue - moshi - hindi - telugu - indic --- # siba · full-duplex speech for Hindi, Telugu and English **siba** is a speech-to-speech dialogue model that listens and speaks at the same time, built by adapting Kyutai's [Moshi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16) to Hindi and Telugu while keeping English. This repository holds the current **Stage 2b** checkpoint plus the Stage 1 base checkpoints it was built from. | | | |---|---| | **Model** | Moshiko (~7.7B parameters, Mimi codec) with a 48k text vocabulary (+16k Hindi/Telugu pieces) | | **Languages** | Hindi, Telugu, English | | **Training** | Stage 1: ~33k h YouTube monologue speech → Stage 2b: 517 h two-channel dialogues, 1,500 steps | | **Agent voices** | one fixed voice per language (Hindi: Ritvik) | | **Status** | research checkpoint — turn-taking works, answer relevance and response speed do not yet | | **Weights** | [`stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors`](stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated) (15.7 GB, bf16) | ## Highlights - **Listens before it speaks.** In Full-Duplex-Bench v1 it stays quiet through 78–81% of the user's mid-sentence pauses, where the original Moshi talks over every one, and it talks over the user in 25% of cases versus 89%. - **Right language, right role.** After dialogue training it replies in the language of the conversation and as an assistant; the Stage 1 model before it monologues, often in the wrong language. - **Still slow and often off-topic.** It takes 1.4–2 s to respond and often does not answer what was asked, especially in Hindi and Telugu (see [Limitations](#limitations)). ## Results ### Full-Duplex-Bench v1 (English) ![Full-Duplex-Bench v1 components, siba Stage 2b vs the original Moshiko](stage2b/assets/fdb_v1.png) | | siba Stage 2b | Moshiko | |---|:---:|:---:| | **Duplex score** (0–100) | **38.4** | **54.5** | | Talks over the user in mid-sentence pauses ↓ | **0.19 – 0.22** | 1.00 | | Talk-over share of all cases ↓ | **0.25** | 0.89 | | Takes the turn when the user finishes ↑ | 0.92 | 1.00 | | Latency to take the turn ↓ | 1.36 s | 0.00 s* | | Yields when interrupted ↑ / latency ↓ | 0.94 / 2.00 s | 0.92 / 0.68 s | | Backchannel frequency ↑ | 0.06 | 0.16 | 25% subset: the first 36 samples of each of the 5 tasks (180), both models run with the same streaming inference. The duplex score is a timing-only composite of the four components (each takes the takeover rate and gives full latency credit at ≤0.3 s, none at ≥2 s); the official GPT relevance judge was not run. \*Moshi's 0 s latency means it was already talking — its higher score partly rewards that. ### Held-out loss ![Held-out first-codebook loss by language during Stage 2b](stage2b/assets/heldout_loss.png) | Step | Hindi | Telugu | English | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 0 (Stage 1, before dialogue training) | 7.94 | 7.69 | 7.71 | | 500 | 0.835 | 0.925 | 0.572 | | **1500 (released)** | **0.807** | **0.904** | **0.562** | 48 held-out one-minute units per language. No overfitting: the final step is the best. ## Quick start ```bash pip install moshi huggingface_hub ``` ```python import torch from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download from moshi.models import loaders, LMGen d = snapshot_download("BNarayanaReddy/siba", allow_patterns=["stage2b/checkpoint_001500/*", "stage2b/tokenizer.model"]) info = loaders.CheckpointInfo.from_hf_repo( "kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16", # Mimi codec moshi_weights=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors", tokenizer=f"{d}/stage2b/tokenizer.model", config_path=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/config.json", ) model = info.get_moshi(device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) mimi = info.get_mimi(device="cuda"); mimi.set_num_codebooks(8) lm_gen = LMGen(model, temp=0.8, temp_text=0.7, top_k=250, top_k_text=25) # Streaming as in Moshi: Mimi-encode the user's audio one 80 ms frame (1920 samples, 24 kHz) at a time; # lm_gen.step(codes) returns the model's text token + audio codes for that frame; mimi.decode() gives its speech. ``` ## Model details
Training data — 45,204 synthetic two-channel dialogues, 517 h | Language | Train hours | Script sources | Agent voice | User voices (vary per dialogue) | |---|:---:|---|---|---| | Hindi | 211 | samvaad-hi-v1, indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), snorbyte | Ritvik | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 male / 60 female) | | Telugu | 178 | indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), Updesh, snorbyte | m3_te_s38 | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 / 60) | | English | 128 | SODA, OpenAssistant | m3_en_s0 | 100 Svarah Indian-English speakers (50 / 50) | Scripts were cleaned (prompts and reasoning stripped, replies capped at ~50 words), voiced with the Maya 3 TTS, force-aligned (MMS) and assembled into two-channel conversations: median turn gap ~0.3 s, ~25% overlapping turn changes, barge-ins where the agent yields within ~0.27 s, and backchannels from a per-voice bank. Audio is Mimi-encoded at 8 codebooks per channel; 473 dialogues (5.6 h) are held out.
Training setup — 1,500 steps on 7 × H100, 31 min | Setting | Value | |---|---| | Init | Stage 1, step 15k (`stage1/checkpoint_015000`) | | Fine-tuning | full, Mimi frozen | | Batch | 49 × 60 s (0.82 h of audio per step), ~2.4 passes over the data | | Optimizer | AdamW, LR 2e-5, one-cycle with 5% warm-up, weight decay 0.1 | | Loss | agent text + agent audio (first codebook ×100, text padding ×0.5); the user channel is input only | | Language weights | Hindi 0.35 · Telugu 0.35 · English 0.30 | Exact config: [`stage2b/args.yaml`](stage2b/args.yaml) · eval log: [`stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl`](stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl) · benchmark reports: [`stage2b/bench/`](stage2b/bench)
Stage 1 (the base) Monologue speech from YouTube — Hindi 12.8k h, Telugu 12.1k h, English 8.4k h — with the user channel silent, so it is not conversational on its own. Checkpoints are in [`stage1/`](stage1) (5k, 10k, 15k; a continuation to 30k is in progress). Stage 2b starts from step 15k.
## Limitations - **Relevance.** Replies are often fluent but not about what the user asked, most of all in Hindi and Telugu. Understanding the user's speech is weak: Stage 1 never had a user channel and Stage 2b adds only ~500 h of listening. Hindi/Telugu knowledge answers can invent facts. - **Latency.** It responds 1.4–2 s after the user finishes, against ~0.3 s gaps in its training data. - **Synthetic data only.** All voices are TTS and the timing is rule-based; no real Hindi/Telugu conversations. Long-answer sources (OpenAssistant, Updesh) give few exchanges per minute. - **Evaluation.** Benchmark numbers are English only and from a 25% subset (components can move by ±0.1). - **Audio.** Moshi's 8-codebook Mimi on top of TTS audio limits clarity. ## Repository contents

The start-of-text row moved to 48000. On original-vocab input, audio logits and the first 32,000 text logits are bit-identical to Moshiko. It turns speech into two streams of integer tokens and decodes them back to 24 kHz audio. It was trained mostly on English and 10 Indian languages, and it is strongest on Indian languages: among codecs at about 1 kbps, it keeps the most words in every one of the 10 we tested. ## Key features - **Low bitrate:** 1.09 kbps, 75 tokens per second. - **Two token streams:** a content stream (25 Hz) that carries the words, and an acoustic stream (50 Hz) that carries the voice and detail. - **Split FSQ, not RVQ:** each stream is a single FSQ grid. Content is coded first, and one acoustic grid codes what remains, instead of a stack of residual codebooks. Each frame is one id per stream, with no learned codebook. - **16 kHz in, 24 kHz out:** any input sample rate is resampled to 16 kHz. - **One file:** all weights are in `model.safetensors`. Nothing else is downloaded. - **Commercial use allowed:** Apache 2.0. All training data is under open licences, none of them non-commercial. ## Model details | | | |---|---| | Content stream | 25 Hz, FSQ 8 × 3 levels = 6,561 ids, 317 bps | | Acoustic stream | 50 Hz, FSQ 6 × 6 levels = 46,656 ids, 775 bps | | Bitrate | 1.09 kbps | | Parameters | 624 M in the file, 387 M of them w2v-BERT 2.0; decoding alone uses 186 M | | Licence | Apache 2.0 | The content stream quantises w2v-BERT 2.0 features (layer 16). The acoustic stream quantises what a CNN encoder hears beyond the content stream. A transformer decoder with an iSTFT head turns the sum back into audio. IndiCodec is built on [NeuCodec](https://huggingface.co/neuphonic/neucodec) by Neuphonic: it uses NeuCodec's architecture, and training started from its released weights. The two-stream quantiser, the encoder training and the training recipe are new. ## Quality Speech codecs at about 1 kbps, on speakers not seen in training. Every codec is scored on the same clips. # pocket-tts-onnx (upstream export)

ONNX graphs for [Kyutai's Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts), exported with
the `export_onnx.py` script that ships with
[VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp](https://github.com/VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp), for use with that C++/ONNX
Runtime runtime.

Six languages: `english_2026-10`, `french_24l`, `german_24l`, `spanish_24l`, `italian_24l`,
`portuguese_24l`. `english_2026-10` (Kyutai's default English model since 2026-10-21, exported with
`pocket-tts` 4.0.1) reads sentence-final numbers again. The older `english_2026-04`, `english_2026-09_2` and
`english_2026-09_24l` folders were removed on 2026-10-29; they stay readable at the earlier commits
(for example `c1f5d6fb`) for anything that still pins one.

## Why this exists

The widely used [KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx](https://huggingface.co/KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx) export
predates PocketTTS.cpp's own exporter. The newer exporter changes the graph, not the weights:

* the Mimi decoder's KV cache is a **circular buffer of 250 positions** instead of 1000, matching
  the model's actual attention context — 4× less masked-out work per decode call;
* K and V caches are **separate tensors**, removing a `torch.stack` copy per step;
* KV caches are stored in **fp16** and bound as both input and output, so ONNX Runtime scatters
  in place instead of copying the cache every step.

Measured on `french_24l`, same runtime binary, same reference voice, INT8 backbone + FP32 flow and
decoder ("mixed" precision), Apple M-series, median of 5 draws over 3 sentences:

| | KevinAHM export | this export |
|---|---|---|
| RTFx | 2.03 | **2.91** |
| first-chunk latency | 723 ms | **294 ms** |
| peak RSS | 1172 MB | **842 MB** |
| Whisper WER (large-v3-turbo, fr) | 0.0 % | **0.0 %** |

Same intelligibility, ~1.4× faster, ~330 MB less resident memory.

## Contents, per language folder

| file | precision | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `flow_lm_main_int8.onnx` | INT8 | backbone; only its MatMuls are quantized, as in Kyutai's own `RECOMMENDED_CONFIG` |
| `flow_lm_flow.onnx` | FP32 | flow-matching net |
| `mimi_decoder.onnx` | FP32 | codec decoder |
| `flow_lm_flow_int8.onnx`, `mimi_decoder_int8.onnx` | INT8 | compact variants, for A/B only |
| `mimi_encoder.onnx`, `text_conditioner.onnx` | FP32 | never quantized upstream |
| `bos_before_voice.npy` | — | learned `[1,1,1024]` vector; **the runtime must prepend it** to the encoded reference voice before conditioning |
| `bundle.json` | — | runtime contract: `model_recommended_frames_after_eos`, `max_token_per_chunk`, `remove_semicolons`, `default_temperature`, plus (session 227) `pocket_tts_version`/`export_script_version` provenance — see below |
| `tokenizer.model` | — | SentencePiece |

Bundles no longer ship `speaker_proj_weight.npy`, `emb_mean.npy` or `emb_std.npy` (the inputs of a
prosody-continuity mode the runtime no longer has): they were removed from every folder on 2026-10-29;
earlier commits still carry them.

`flow_lm_main.onnx` (FP32, 1.2 GB per language) is not published — it is only needed to validate the
INT8 quantization, which was done at export time.

### Quantizing INT8 Mimi is not free

The INT8 Mimi decoder is included for comparison, not recommended. Against the FP32 decoder on
identical latents it scores ~16.5 dB SNR, and the error is chunk-size dependent (ONNX Runtime derives
the activation scale from the chunk), correlated with the signal, and concentrated in 2–5 kHz —
audible roughness. Kyutai's own runtime never quantizes Mimi or the flow net.

## Reproducing

The upstream script is hardcoded to the 6-layer `b6369a24` English checkpoint, whose config no longer
ships with `pocket_tts` (upstream issue #12). Two changes were needed:

1. derive `FlowLMMainWrapper.NUM_LAYERS` from `len(flow_lm.transformer.layers)` — the `*_24l`
   checkpoints have 24 layers, and a hardcoded 6 silently drops 18 layers' worth of state;
2. select the config by language and let `pocket_tts` resolve the `hf://…@rev` weights.

Every export was validated against PyTorch, FP32 and INT8, with the script's own `run_validation`.

### Provenance (session 227)

Every `bundle.json` now records `pocket_tts_version` (the installed `pocket-tts` package's release
version, or `<version>+git<sha12>` when installed straight from a git ref via pip's PEP 610
`direct_url.json`) and `export_script_version` (a dated stamp bumped whenever
`tools/pockettts_export/export_onnx.py`'s export-affecting logic changes) — before this, a downloaded
bundle's staleness relative to either the upstream package or this repo's own export tooling was not
verifiable without re-running the exporter from scratch. `default_temperature` is also recorded per
language (`0.3` for English per Kyutai's own commit `d108410`, `null`/absent elsewhere — see the
runtime's `Bundle::default_temperature` for how a bundle without the key falls back unchanged).

## Licence and attribution

Weights © Kyutai, released under **CC-BY-4.0**; these are derived works (ONNX conversions) and carry
the same licence. Source model: <https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts>. Export tooling:
VolgaGerm/PocketTTS.cpp (MIT).

# Swar: open Nepali voice cloning

Swar speaks Nepali the way it is spoken in Nepal and clones a voice from 20 to 30 seconds of someone talking. It reads Nepali, English, and Nepali mixed with English. By [Naamche Labs](https://github.com/Naamche-Labs).

**Try it free:** [Colab notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/Naamche-Labs/swar/blob/main/notebooks/Swar_Clone_Colab.ipynb) (free T4 GPU). **Code and paper:** [github.com/Naamche-Labs/swar](https://github.com/Naamche-Labs/swar).

## Files

- `podvoices_ema.pt`: **the default model** (F5-TTS Base architecture, EMA weights). Every result below is this file.
- `swar_v6_ema.pt`: a second checkpoint for English-heavy text, trained further with 96 h of English (LibriTTS-R). Mixed Nepali-English errors 5.24% (default 5.6%), but pure Nepali is weaker (NepTTS-Bench pronunciation error 4.04%, FLEURS cloning errors 5.41%). Use it with `ENGLISH_LATIN=1`.
- `vocab.txt`: character vocabulary (IndicF5).
- `kriti_onnx/`: Kriti, our Nepali speech recogniser (MIT), used to transcribe uploads and check takes.
- `presets/`: ready voices Maya (female) and Aarav (male), built only from model-made audio.
- `app/`: the cloner app (Gradio) used by the notebook.

## Results (NepTTS-Bench, 205 sentences, one take)

| System | Character error | Pronunciation error | UTMOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Swar, studio voice | **6.19** | **2.92** | 3.82 |
| Swar, Maya voice | 7.45 | 4.52 | **4.09** |
| OmniVoice (same prompt) | 6.68 | 4.32 | 3.93 |
| Indic-Speak Srijana | 10.25 | 8.12 | 3.97 |
| ElevenLabs v3 | 15.70 | 12.91 | |

[Nepali Voice Cloning Benchmark](https://github.com/Naamche-Labs/nepali-voice-cloning-bench) (our open benchmark on FLEURS, v1.1, clean track, 64 distinct prompt + sentence pairs from 4 unseen voices): Swar errors 4.72% and voice match 0.697, OmniVoice 5.08% and 0.683, IndicF5 8.30% and 0.669.

Nepali mixed with English (30 held-out sentences): Swar 5.6% character errors, OmniVoice 11.4%. UTMOS is an automatic predictor, not a listener test.

## Training data

Initialised from ai4bharat/IndicF5 (MIT). Fine-tuned on AI4Bharat Rasa and IndicVoices-R (CC BY 4.0), Google FLEURS (CC BY 4.0), OpenSLR 43 and 54 (CC BY-SA 4.0), LibriTTS-R (CC BY 4.0), and podcast speech used with the speakers' permission (not released). The weights are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 to respect the share-alike data.

## Responsible use

Only clone a voice with that person's permission. Do not use Swar to impersonate anyone, to deceive, or to commit fraud.

# Chatterbox Nano Core AI · compact mixed palettes

Experimental English narration and voice enrollment for iOS 27+ and macOS 27+
on Apple Silicon. Five native `.aimodel` assets, converted and optimized by
**Ron Bakker** from [Resemble AI Chatterbox Nano](https://huggingface.co/ResembleAI/chatterbox-nano).
Output is mono 24 kHz PCM. Voices and recordings are not included.

| Components | Files before archive compression |
|---|---:|
| Four narration models and required tables | 408.5 MB |
| Optional combined voice enrollment | 188.0 MB |

Uses 8-bit palettes for selected narration and enrollment weights, with one
T3 projection in 4-bit storage. Sensitive T3 matrices and the vocoder retain
FP16; frontends and speaker networks retain their original precision.
Palette values are FP16 and computation remains floating point. Expression
can differ from the FP16 version. See [weight-formats.json](weight-formats.json)
and [INTEGRATION.md](INTEGRATION.md).

## Measured warm performance

| Device | OS | Median RTF | Three-run range |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| iPhone 16 Pro | iOS 27.0.1 | 0.204 | 0.198–0.205 |
| M1 Max | macOS 27.0.1 | 0.176 | 0.164–0.177 |

One prepared English sentence, 6.40 s on iPhone and
6.28 s on Mac, with three retained warm repeats.
RTF is completed text-to-PCM synthesis wall divided by generated audio duration,
including sampling, cache updates, acoustic input writes, solver work and output
reads/waits. Loading/compilation, fixed conditioning/random-input preparation,
one complete warm-up, WAV writing and playback are excluded. Enrollment is
separate. Other text lengths and shapes can perform differently.

Conversion, optimization and packaging: Copyright (c) 2026 Ron Bakker.

# DRAMA-3 · T8 native models

[English](#english) | [简体中文](#简体中文)

## English

Converted weights for [ComfyUI-Drama3-T8](https://github.com/T8mars/Comfyui-Drama-3) and its local voice studio. Built with Fish Audio. Use the T8 native loader; these files are not Transformers checkpoints. W4A8, compact control heads and the native single-file aligner require code 0.2.0 or later.

| File | Size | ComfyUI destination / purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| `drama3-t8-fp8.safetensors` | 38.58 GB | `models/diffusion_models/` — main model |
| `drama3-t8-w4a8.safetensors` | 24.60 GB | Same folder — optional smaller main model |
| `drama3-codec.safetensors` | 1.57 GB | `models/vae/` — audio Codec |
| `drama3-line-head.safetensors` | 8.48 KB | `models/diffusion_models/` — compact Scene/control head |
| `drama3-text-head.safetensors` | 1.03 GB | Same folder — full-head alternative/fallback |
| `qwen3-asr-06b.safetensors` | 1.56 GB | `models/asr/` — optional transcription |
| `qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors` | 4.08 GB | Same folder — optional larger ASR |
| `qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16.safetensors` | 1.84 GB | `models/asr/` — optional word timing |
| `Confucius4-R2T2-GGUF/` | 2.18 GB | `models/asr/` — model plus matching projector |
| `FireRedVAD-ONNX/` | 2.31 MB model | `models/asr/` — optional segmented R2T2 |

Choose one main model plus Codec and the head needed by your workflow. Compact Scene mode uses the small line-head, with the full text/control head as fallback. The complete `qwen-aligner/` directory remains an alternative to the single-file aligner. Download complete auxiliary folders; keep the R2T2 model/projector together. W6A8/INT8 are available through code-side local conversion, not this upload.

All paths are configurable, including absolute paths on other drives. Studio uses its own `models/` folder. Voice conditioning uses reference audio with a matching transcript; a manual transcript needs no ASR. GitHub code/node assets contain neither model weights nor bundled Python; the R2T2 native runtime is distributed separately.

Supported dependencies: **Transformers 4.57.1 / tokenizers 0.22.2 / huggingface-hub 0.36.2**, with **Torch 2.8 + CUDA 12.8**. Other dependency combinations are not covered. Local checks used Windows x64, RTX 5090 Laptop, 24 GB VRAM / 64 GB RAM; cache size is not total memory consumption.

Use [ComfyUI-Drama3-T8](https://github.com/T8mars/Comfyui-Drama-3) 0.2.4 for the tested audio-tower attention fix and CUDA Graph residency precheck. The inference code follows Fish Audio's grouped tower path; model weights and filenames are unchanged, so this update does not require downloading a new checkpoint. If normalization weights remain offloaded, generation uses eager execution and records the reason before capture.
